items.title: NSA’s PROMIS: What the Declassified Records Actually Show
items.summary: PROMIS has accumulated decades of controversy, competing claims and, at times, confusion over what the name itself actually refers to. The records released by the National Security Agency provide an important distinction. The NSA’s PROMIS, or Product Management Information System, was an intelligence-product management database developed during the 1970s. According to records released to The Black Vault under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), the system was designed to organize information associated with intelligence reports and give senior signals intelligence managers a way to search, analyze and manage information about those products. It should not simply be equated with the better-known Prosecutor’s Management Information System, also called PROMIS, associated with INSLAW, Inc. and the Department of Justice. That distinction became a central issue when the Justice Department investigated allegations surrounding INSLAW and its software in the 1990s. DOJ ultimately concluded in 1994 that there was no credible evidence that INSLAW’s PROMIS had been improperly distributed elsewhere in the federal government or to foreign governments. A subsequent Court of Federal Claims proceeding also rejected INSLAW’s claims. Yet NSA did, in fact, have something called PROMIS. The records obtained by The Black Vault document what it was, and then a FOIA request filed in 2013 to uncover those records produced one final surprise nearly 13 years later. items.title: NSA Releases Heavily Redacted 1972 Technical Journal Article After Nine-Year FOIA Wait
items.summary: More than nine years after a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request was submitted to the National Security Agency, the agency has released a heavily redacted copy of a 1972 NSA Technical Journal article titled “Maybe It’s Related to the Phase of the Moon…” The Black Vault submitted the request on August 6, 2017, seeking the article, which was published in the Fall 1972 edition of the journal. The NSA ultimately processed the request as FOIA Case 102240 and issued its response on August 25, 2026. The article, written by Herbert S. Guy, Jr., concerns the analysis of a callsign system. The portion released on the opening page describes it as “the story of the dissection of a callsign system” and discusses the overlapping work of cryptanalysts, traffic analysts and linguists. However, only a relatively small portion of the underlying article is readable in the release. Large sections, including entire pages, remain withheld. In its response, the NSA stated that the withheld material is exempt under FOIA Exemption 3 , which permits withholding information protected from disclosure by another federal statute. According to the agency: “The specific statute applicable in this case is Section 6, Public Law 86-36 ( 50 U.S. Code 3605 ).” The NSA further stated that it “reasonably foresees that disclosure of the withheld information would be harmful to an interest that is protected by the identified exemption.” The Black Vault intends to appeal the redactions and seek additional…

Suspected Military Retrieval and Witness Accounts Project Blue Book Files: The Official Investigation NASA’s Involvement and the Missing “Fragology” Files New Findings via The Black Vault (2021 FOIA Releases) Conclusion Executive Summary The Kecksburg UFO incident of December 9, 1965 remains one of the most intriguing unresolved cases of a mysterious object falling from the sky. Often dubbed “Pennsylvania’s Roswell,” it involved reports of a fiery fireball streaking over several U.S. states and Canada, a crash in the woods near the village of Kecksburg, and an alleged military recovery of an unknown object [1] . Over the decades, the incident has been the subject of intense speculation – from meteor to secret Cold War satellite to extraterrestrial craft – and persistent efforts by investigators to unearth official records. This deep dive examines all angles of the Kecksburg case, drawing on eyewitness accounts, media reports, and released government documents (many obtained via The Black Vault’s FOIA requests) to present a balanced, evidence-backed picture of what we know. items.title: The Pangram Paradox: The Problem with AI “Detecting” other AIs
items.summary: Op-ed: This is an opinion piece published on Unlimited Hangout . Most articles published on UH are not opinion pieces, so we are clearly labeling those that are. It should be no secret to readers of Unlimited Hangout that I have a very negative view of the impact that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is having on independent media and media in general. As someone who has been impersonated by AI daily on large video platforms for a few years now, I have come to acutely feel that AI is becoming a dangerous force that is making it increasingly difficult for well-meaning readers/viewers to distinguish between what is real and what is false. I don’t mean just for those hoping to view my content, as the personal issue I am facing is a microcosm of a much larger problem. As a result, one might think that I would have been pleased, if not relieved, to see Substack, a large platform for professional writers, partner with an “AI detection tool.” Not only am I not pleased, but I have now taken the time to write an opinion piece explaining why I think this is bad and to also explain where I think a lot of this is going. Substack’s new partner and, apparently, the AI detection tool of choice for most major media outlets right now is called Pangram. Pangram was founded in 2023, originally under the name Checkfor.ai, by Max Spero and Bradley Emi. items.title: FOI documents on origins of Covid-19,  gain-of-function research and biolabs
items.summary: For more information about our investigation, see our reporting on COVID-19 origins , gain-of-function research and other high-risk virology research . Here are the documents we have obtained on these subjects so far from Freedom of Information requests. The documents are posted below in approximately the chronological order in which we received them. We have filed 298 state, federal, and international public records requests, and 46 FOI lawsuits , seeking information about the origins of SARS-CoV-2 and the risks of biosafety labs and gain-of-function research. As of September 1, 2026, U.S. Right to Know has obtained and published more than 280,000 pages of public records related to COVID-19 origins, gain-of-function research and biosafety. In July 2020, U.S. Right to Know began submitting public records requests in pursuit of data from public institutions in an effort to discover what is known about the origins of the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which causes the disease Covid-19. We are also researching accidents, leaks and other mishaps at laboratories where pathogens of pandemic potential are stored and modified, and the risks of gain-of-function research, which involve experiments on such pathogens to increase their host range, infectivity, transmissibility or pathogenicity. items.title: Ralph Baric warned COVID statement could be used for ‘nefarious purposes to shift blame,’ email shows
items.summary: In early February 2020, as scientists and U.S. intelligence officials scrambled to understand the origins of the emerging coronavirus, prominent virologist Ralph Baric was asked to make a public statement knocking down claims that a chimeric coronavirus created in his University of North Carolina laboratory using genetic material supplied by a Wuhan scientist was the virus causing the outbreak. Baric thought the scientific answer was straightforward. The viruses differed by more than 5,000 nucleotides, the individual building blocks that make up a viral sequence, he wrote, adding the chimeric viruses created at his laboratory “were never sent to china.” But what appeared to worry him more was how his statement might be used. In a Feb. 6 email to a group of scientists who advise U.S. intelligence agencies, Baric said the requested statement could help rebut claims circulating on Chinese social media. But, he warned, it also could be used for “nefarious purposes to shift blame.” “I have received a few concerning, if not threatening, emails,” Baric wrote. He said he had informed his university and advised the group he “believe[d] that you should be informed as well.” The email, which was among records recently obtained by U.S. Right To Know, through an ongoing Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, does not identify who asked Baric to make the statement, and it does not say whose blame he feared might be shifted, or onto…

items.title: Critiques of Gates Foundation’s agricultural interventions in Africa
items.summary: The Gates Foundation is a major influencer and funder of agricultural development in Africa, yet there are no meaningful avenues to hold it accountable to the communities it affects. The foundation is the main funder of the controversial AGRA program (formerly the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa). AGRA rebranded in 2022 after evidence-based critiques — including its own internal review — found that AGRA’s 15-year effort to expand industrial agriculture in Africa has failed to improve food security, despite billions in aid from private donors and government subsidies. Critics, including many Africa-based groups and faith leaders, say the “green revolution” approach — expanding chemical-intensive, monoculture farming geared toward export-oriented commodity crops — is exacerbating hunger, worsening inequality and entrenching corporate power in the hungriest regions of the world. This fact sheet links to research and news articles documenting these concerns. See more of our reporting on Bill Gates and the Gates Foundation’s influence on food systems . items.excerpt: The Gates Foundation is a major influencer and funder of agricultural development in Africa, yet there are no meaningful avenues to hold it accountable to the communities it affects. The foundation is the main funder of the controversial AGRA program (formerly the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa). AGRA rebranded in 2022 after evidence-based critiques — including its own internal review — found that AGRA’s 15-year effort to expand industrial agriculture in Africa has failed to improve food security, despite billions in aid from private donors and government subsidies.
